power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Conceptualizing Duration: A Corpus-Based Study of Distance and Quantity Metaphors of Time in Japanese

text.text: The modern study of conceptual metaphors in cognitive science is grounded in Lakoff and Johnson's (1980) seminal work.
text.formatted: The modern study of conceptual metaphors in cognitive science is grounded in <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Lakoff and Johnson's (1980)</ref> seminal work.

text.text: They propose that metaphors are not merely rhetorical flourishes but a fundamental cognitive mechanism that allows speakers to understand abstract concepts in terms of more experiential or concrete domains.
For instance, time is often conceptualized through spatial terms such as before, after, long, short, near, or far.
Similarly, time can be framed as a resource or substance that may be spent, wasted, or accumulated, thus motivating quantity or amount metaphors.
Conceptual Metaphor Theory (Lakoff & Johnson, 1980 , 1999) holds that abstract concepts are organized by metaphorical mappings grounded in bodily and sensorimotor experience.
text.formatted: Conceptual Metaphor Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Lakoff & Johnson, 1980</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">, 1999)</ref> holds that abstract concepts are organized by metaphorical mappings grounded in bodily and sensorimotor experience.

text.text: Linguistic expressions serve as primary evidence for these mappings, and systematic analysis of recurring idioms and constructions enables researchers to infer the underlying cognitive structure.
From this perspective, speakers in different language communities are likely to differ in the relative dominance of the mappings on which they rely.
Speakers of different languages may rely on partially distinct metaphors, leading to cross-linguistic similarities and differences in how time is expressed (Radden, 2004).
text.formatted: Speakers of different languages may rely on partially distinct metaphors, leading to cross-linguistic similarities and differences in how time is expressed <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Radden, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Over the past several decades, numerous studies have examined the extent to which such linguistic variations correlate with differences in cognition; an approach sometimes referred to as linguistic relativity.
Within the domain of time, two particularly salient metaphors stand out.
First, time-as-distance views duration as an extension in space.
In English, for instance, it is common to hear a long time, a short wait, or a lengthy discussion, all of which transfer spatial properties of length onto the temporal dimension.
Second, timeas-quantity treats duration more like quantity: much time, a lot of time, or little time.
While English employs both forms, studies often highlight that distance metaphors are more conventional and preferable, and this tendency is often seen in Germanic languages.
In contrast, other languages more readily use quantity metaphors for time.
Spanish speakers, for example, rarely say largo tiempo ("long time"); instead, they typically use mucho tiempo ("much time") to convey extended duration (Casasanto, 2005; Boroditsky, 2011).
text.formatted: Spanish speakers, for example, rarely say largo tiempo ("long time"); instead, they typically use mucho tiempo ("much time") to convey extended duration <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Casasanto, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Boroditsky, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This difference is so marked that Spanish-English bilinguals sometimes show distinct patterns of temporal reasoning depending on whether they are tested in English or Spanish (Bylund & Athanasopoulos, 2017; 2023).
text.formatted: This difference is so marked that Spanish-English bilinguals sometimes show distinct patterns of temporal reasoning depending on whether they are tested in English or Spanish <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bylund & Athanasopoulos, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">2023)</ref>.

text.text: Greek is another commonly cited case:
Greek speakers favor big or small as descriptors for duration, such as megali ora ("big hour"), rather than long or short (Casasanto, 2016).
text.formatted: Greek speakers favor big or small as descriptors for duration, such as megali ora ("big hour"), rather than long or short <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Casasanto, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: To gain a broad understanding of how different metaphors for time are used across languages, Casasanto (2005) conducted a simple corpus-based survey using Google search hit counts.
text.formatted: To gain a broad understanding of how different metaphors for time are used across languages, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Casasanto (2005)</ref> conducted a simple corpus-based survey using Google search hit counts.

text.text: The target languages were English, Spanish, Greek, and Indonesian.
The results showed that in English and Indonesian, metaphors based on spatial distance were overwhelmingly more frequent.
In contrast, in Spanish and Greek, quantity-based metaphors were more common, and distance metaphors were rarely used.
This pattern has since been frequently cited as cross-linguistic typological evidence regarding metaphors for duration.

In recent years, many empirical psychological experiments have investigated whether the concept of time is mapped onto space, as suggested by metaphors (e.g., Boroditsky, 2001; Boroditsky, Fuhrman, & McCormick, 2011; Fuhrman et al., 2011; Gentner, Imai, & Boroditsky, 2002; Ulrich et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In recent years, many empirical psychological experiments have investigated whether the concept of time is mapped onto space, as suggested by metaphors (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Boroditsky, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Boroditsky, Fuhrman, & McCormick, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Fuhrman et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Gentner, Imai, & Boroditsky, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Ulrich et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Some psychophysical experiments suggest that the metaphors a language uses for duration guide the attention people give to different spatial cues when judging time.

In a series of non-linguistic trials, Casasanto and Boroditsky (2008) asked monolingual English adults to watch animated lines that varied in how far they grew and how long they stayed on the screen (these lines functioned as distractors); when the task was to assess and reproduce the elapsed time, longer lines made the same interval feel longer.
text.formatted: In a series of non-linguistic trials, <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Casasanto and Boroditsky (2008)</ref> asked monolingual English adults to watch animated lines that varied in how far they grew and how long they stayed on the screen (these lines functioned as distractors); when the task was to assess and reproduce the elapsed time, longer lines made the same interval feel longer.

text.text: Building on the same logic, Bylund and Athanasopoulos (2017) compared Swedish speakers, whose language talks about a long or short time, with Spanish speakers, who talk about much or little time, and they used both a growing-line display and a filling-container display.
text.formatted: Building on the same logic, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Bylund and Athanasopoulos (2017)</ref> compared Swedish speakers, whose language talks about a long or short time, with Spanish speakers, who talk about much or little time, and they used both a growing-line display and a filling-container display.

text.text: When each trial began with a brief prompt in the participant's own language, Swedish participants were distracted mainly by line length, Spanish participants mainly by fill level, and balanced bilinguals switched between the two patterns according to the language of the prompt.

Taken together, these findings show that habitual linguistic framing (long/short versus much/little) cultivates different but flexible attentional habits that can bias basic duration judgments without fixing them permanently.
That is, speakers of a given language tend to habitually conceptualize duration according to the metaphors prevalent in their language.
For speakers who regularly describe time in terms of spatial distance (e.g., long time, short wait), this metaphorical framing becomes a habitual cognitive pattern.

As a result, they are more susceptible to being influenced by spatial cues that align with or interfere with that habitual pattern, such as the length of a distracting line, even in non-linguistic tasks.

Conversely, speakers accustomed to conceptualizing time in terms of quantity (e.g., much time, little time) show greater sensitivity to cues related to amount, such as the level of a filling container.
In comparison to English, Spanish, or Greek, the question of whether Japanese favors distance-or quantity-based duration metaphors has attracted relatively limited attention in the previous studies.
Many Japanese linguistics and cognitive semantics studies have instead focused on motion metaphors of time.

For instance, whether time is conceptualized as moving toward the ego (締め切りが迫る shimekiri-ga semaru: "the deadline is coming") or the ego moving through time (締め切りに近づく shimekiri-ni chikazuku: "we are approaching the deadline": Masuko, 2019; Suzuki, 2015).
text.formatted: For instance, whether time is conceptualized as moving toward the ego (締め切りが迫る shimekiri-ga semaru: "the deadline is coming") or the ego moving through time (締め切りに近づく shimekiri-ni chikazuku: "we are approaching the deadline": <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Masuko, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Suzuki, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: It is also pointed out that Japanese also has rich temporal metaphors involving upward and downward directions, attributing this to the metaphor of a river in time expressions.

She observed that in Japanese temporal expressions (e.g., 時間をさかのぼる jikan-o sakanoboru "go upstream in time," 時間を下る jikan-o kudaru "go downstream in time"), the past is mapped as upward and behind, while the future is mapped as downward and forward (Seto, 1995; Shinohara, 2013 Shinohara, , 2020)).
text.formatted: She observed that in Japanese temporal expressions (e.g., 時間をさかのぼる jikan-o sakanoboru "go upstream in time," 時間を下る jikan-o kudaru "go downstream in time"), the past is mapped as upward and behind, while the future is mapped as downward and forward <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Seto, 1995;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Shinohara, 2013</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Shinohara, , 2020))</ref>.

text.text: While these aspects of temporal framing are certainly relevant to understanding Japanese conceptualizations of time, the specific question of how durations are typically described, whether as "long/short" or as "much/little", has not been examined as thoroughly.

Japanese permits both spatial descriptors for duration (長い時間 nagai jikan: "long time") and (短い時間 mijikai jikan: "short time") as well as amount-based descriptors (多くの時間 ookuno jikan: "much time" and 少ない時間 sukunai jikan: "little time").
However, both quantitybased and distance-based expressions for time are typically present within an individual language.
As mentioned above, English tends to favor distance-based expressions such as long time over quantity-based ones like much time, but the latter is not entirely unacceptable.
This issue of preference cannot be determined simply by examining whether a particular expression is grammatically possible in the target language.
To clarify such patterns, a corpus-based approach is highly effective.
By extracting and analyzing adjectives that co-occur with "time" (i.e., 時間 jikan 1 ), it may be possible to reveal the usage tendencies and preferences in Japanese.
This study uses the Balanced Corpus of Contemporary Written Japanese (BCCWJ) Version 1.1, developed by the National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics (Maekawa et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This study uses the Balanced Corpus of Contemporary Written Japanese (BCCWJ) Version 1.1, developed by the National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Maekawa et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The BCCWJ is the only balanced corpus currently available for contemporary written Japanese and was designed to provide a comprehensive overview of written language use across a variety of domains.
The corpus includes texts published in Japan, covering newspapers, magazines, and a wide range of books including fiction, non-fiction, official reports, and textbooks.
In addition, it contains a small number of texts from online sources, such as Q&A discussion boards.
text.formatted: In addition, it contains a small number of texts from online sources, such as Q&A discussion boards.

text.text: The total size of the corpus is approximately 104 million words, with samples randomly drawn from each genre to ensure representativeness.
The publication years of the materials span up to 30 years , with the majority of book data drawn from the period between 1986 and 2005.
By incorporating multiple genres and publication types across several decades, the BCCWJ enables a broad and balanced view of lexical and grammatical patterns in contemporary written Japanese.
The BCCWJ is available in several different formats.
The main differences between the formats are whether the format uses fixed-or variable-length sampling, and whether the data is provided in a token-per-line format or sentenceper-line format.
Fixed-length sampling takes a random character from the original text as a starting position and takes 1,000 characters from the starting position for each sample.
Variable-length sampling takes a random character and uses the whole linguistic construction including that character, up to 10,000 characters, as one sample.

In order to use the maximum amount of data available, the present study selected the M-XML format, which combines data from variable-and fixedlength sampling and removes overlap, and is in sentence-per-line format which was more convenient for the extraction procedure.
In order to cut down on the processing time, only the sentences including words whose lemma form is 時間 jikan ('time') were included in the following procedure.
In order to extract expressions related to time, the present study employed UniDic2UD, a dependency parser for modern and contemporary Japanese (Yasuoka, 2020).
text.formatted: In order to extract expressions related to time, the present study employed UniDic2UD, a dependency parser for modern and contemporary Japanese <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Yasuoka, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The parser takes in an unannotated string as input and returns a list of the tokens in the string along with information such as their lemma form, part of speech, and phonetic reading.
The parser also provides the indices of the governing tokens in the dependency relationships.
An example is provided in Figure 1.
text.formatted: An example is provided in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: In this case, わずか wazuka ('a small amount') is dependent on 時間 jikan ('time'), so the seventh column in the わずか entry (token 2) points to token 4, the 時間 entry.
Although BCCWJ's M-XML data is in XML format, all XML tags were removed before running UniDic2UD, as the default use of UniDic2UD requires raw sentences without annotations.

Each sentence output by UniDic2UD was then scanned for the index of the word 時間 jikan ('time') and for words with the ADJ (adjective) part-of-speech tag which pointed to the index of 時間, resulting in a list of adjectives dependent on the word 時間.

In the context of Universal Dependencies, the ADJ tag is usually assigned to words that specify properties or attributes of nouns (Universal Dependencies contributors, 2024), and the present study will use this definition when referring to adjectives.
As outlined in Section 3.2, all adjectives that bear a dependency relation to the noun 時間 jikan 'time' were extracted.

Adjectives that appeared at least twice in the corpus were then inspected manually, and any form that could plausibly realize a distance-or amount-based metaphor for duration was provisionally retained.

Adjectives such as 厳しい kibishii ('harsh'; 2 instances), 微妙な bimyo na ('subtle'; 2 instances), and 適度な tekido na ('moderate'; 2 instances) possibly reflect durational metaphor, but were excluded from the analysis because they cannot be clearly classified as either distance-based or amount-based.

Similarly, adjectives such as 無駄な muda na ('wasteful/waste of'; 55 instances), 充分/十分な jubun na ('sufficient'; 45 instances), 半端な hampa-na ('incomplete'; 22 instances), 余計 な yokei na ("unnecessary"; 8 instances), and 余 分 な yobun na ("excess"; 6 instances) were also excluded, as it was difficult to determine whether they reflected a distance metaphor, an amount metaphor, or potentially both.
The counts above represent the total number of instances, including all variations in written form.
Next, the immediate sentential context of every retained token was examined.
An expression was kept only if the adjective-時間 jikan pairing clearly described duration.
Thus, occurrences that involved distance or amount imagery but referred to a point in time rather than duration were removed.
For example, 夕方近い時 間 yuugata chikai jikan "a time close to evening" uses the distance adjective 近 い chikai "near", yet it pinpoints a moment on the daily timeline; such tokens were excluded.

We also discarded strings in which the metaphorical interpretation applied to a subsequent verb instead of to 時間 itself (e.g., ki no tooku naru you na jikan 気の遠くなるような時間 'time so long it makes one feel faint' or は てしなく時間がかかる hateshi naku jikan-ga kakaru "it takes boundless time").

Likewise, cases where the adjective-noun pair alone was insufficient to determine the metaphor type, for instance 十分な時間を置く juubun na jikan-o oku or 十 分な時間を取る juubun na jikan-o toru (both "take enough time"), which rely on the verb to convey an amount metaphor were set aside, because the present study focuses exclusively on adjective-noun pairs.
Variations in orthography, such as between kanji and hiragana (e.g., 長い vs.
ながい = nagai), as well as expressive elongations using long vowel marks (e.g., なが～い = nagaai), were consolidated into the same category.
Note, however, that there were only two instances of tokens with such expressive elongations.
After these cleaning steps, two definitive lists were compiled: one of distancebased duration metaphors and one of amount-based duration metaphors.
Token frequencies for the two sets were then compared to determine which metaphor type predominates in Japanese usage.
The results are shown in Table 1.
text.formatted: The results are shown in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: The analysis yielded a total of 3,057 tokens in which adjectives co-occurred with the noun 時間 jikan ("time") in contexts clearly indicating duration.
These tokens were classified into two types of metaphorical framing: distance-based and amount-based.
We identified 1,035 tokens of distance-amount metaphorical expressions (distance: 839, amount: 196).
Among the distance-based expressions, the adjective 長い nagai ("long") was by far the most frequent, appearing in 597 instances.
The second most frequent was 短い mijikai ("short"), which occurred 222 times.
When combined with lowerfrequency expressions such as 長く nagaku, 短く mijikaku, 短め mijikame, and 長大 choudai, the total number of distance metaphor tokens reached 843.
This strongly suggests that Japanese temporal expressions predominantly conceptualize duration as an extension in space.

very long 2 distance Note. *1: predicative form, *2: past/negative form (e.g., 長かった時間 nagakatta jikan, 短くない時間 mijikak-u nai jikan) In contrast, amount-based expressions were more lexically diverse but considerably less frequent overall.
The most frequent among them was わずか wazuka ("a small amount"), which appeared 121 times.

Other terms such as 膨大 boudai ("huge amount"), 少ない sukunai ("little"), 多大 tadai ("large amount"), たくさん takusan ("a lot"), and 莫大 bakudai ("immense") occurred with much lower frequency, ranging from 7 to 29 tokens each.
The combined total for amount-based expressions was 196 tokens, less than one quarter of the frequency observed for distance-based expressions.
This distribution suggests that, although Japanese permits both types of metaphorical framing, speakers overwhelmingly favor distance metaphors when describing duration.
Additionally, the analysis included surface variants and orthographic differences such as hiragana and kanji alternations (e.g., 長い vs.
ながい [nagai]), as well as expressive elongations involving long vowel marks for emphasis (e.g., な が ～ い [nagaai]).
These were normalized and counted within the same categories.
It should be noted, however, that expressive variants with elongation were rare, with only two instances found in the entire dataset.
This study examined whether Japanese speakers prefer distance or amount metaphors when describing temporal duration, using a large-scale corpus analysis of adjective-noun pairings.
Distance metaphors accounted for about 80% of all 1,035 tokens, whereas amount metaphors comprised roughly 20%.
This distribution mirrors the long-short preference reported for English and German and contrasts with the much-little preference noted for Spanish and Greek.

Consistent with previous studies motivated by Lakoff and Johnson's conceptual metaphor framework, languages dominated by distance metaphors tend to show greater interference from spatial length cues in timing tasks.
text.formatted: Consistent with previous studies motivated by <ref type="bibr">Lakoff and</ref> Johnson's conceptual metaphor framework, languages dominated by distance metaphors tend to show greater interference from spatial length cues in timing tasks.

text.text: Although few psychophysical experiments have examined Japanese speakers, the linguistic evidence presented here suggests that they may pattern with English speakers in this respect.
The present data do not permit a definitive explanation for the relative scarcity of amount metaphors, yet pragmatic selectivity is a plausible factor.

Distance metaphors draw on broadly applicable adjectives such as 長い nagai "long" and 短い mijikai "short," whereas amount metaphors rely more on evaluative items like わずか wazuka "slight" and 膨大 boudai "enormous," whose use may be confined to formal prose or emphatic contexts.
In addition, the analysis was restricted to adjective-noun pairs, excluding verb-dependent amount expressions such as 少し時間がかかる (sukoshi jikan ga kakaru "take a little time").

Incorporating such verb phrases would likely increase the share of amount metaphors, but doing so would also complicate the criteria for classifying metaphor types; limiting the survey to adjectives therefore maintains theoretical coherence.
This study provides a more detailed analysis than previous studies and should serve as a reference point for future research.

Although Casasanto (2005) is frequently cited as a typological source for duration metaphors, his study was limited to comparing the number of web search hits for four adjectives-long, short, much, and little.
text.formatted: Although <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Casasanto (2005)</ref> is frequently cited as a typological source for duration metaphors, his study was limited to comparing the number of web search hits for four adjectives-long, short, much, and little.

text.text: This approach may fail to capture the rich lexical oppositions identified in the present study.
In languages with a more fine-grained lexicon, low-frequency items tend to be underestimated, and the method does not account for pragmatic distinctions or syntactic constraints.

Future research should employ parallel corpora consisting of equivalent content in multiple languages and extract adjectives directly modifying temporal nouns using morphological analysis and dependency parsing.
This would allow for a classification of distance-based and quantity-based metaphors while preserving lexical diversity.
The dominance of distance-based versus quantity-based metaphors should be understood as a matter of degree, rather than a categorical distinction.

Even if distance-based expressions are more frequent in Japanese, the extent to which this preference differs from that of English or other languages assumed to favor quantity-based expressions cannot be determined without a shared basis of comparison.

By comparing the frequency ratio of distance-and quantity-based metaphors across languages using a common metric, it becomes possible to uncover subtle differences that have been overlooked in previous binary classifications.

Moreover, treating metaphorical dominance based on corpus frequency as a continuous variable and aligning it with experimental data, such as temporal judgment tasks, would allow for a more precise assessment of the relationship between lexical preferences and cognitive effects.

In sum, the present investigation offers the first quantitative evidence that distance metaphors dominate duration talk in Japanese and, by extension, supplies a new data point for conceptual metaphor theory and linguistic relativity.

Extending the current analysis, conducting parallel corpus comparisons, and performing experiments based on corpus frequencies will help build a more complete picture of how human cognition in general represents time across languages.
Note 1 A preliminary survey revealed that adjectives co-occurring with 時 toki rarely reflect duration metaphors.
Instead, 時 toki tends to denote temporal points, often in the context of subordinate clauses (e.g., 私が小さい時に watashi-ga chiisai toki-ni "when I was a child").
Consequently, adjectives such as 小さい chiisai "small" or 大きい ookii "big" in these constructions typically describe the subject's state rather than the temporal duration.
In contrast, 時間 jikan more readily functions as a scalar quantity, making it semantically and syntactically more compatible with distance or quantity metaphors.
